{{short description|Measure of relativistic velocity}}
[[File:Inverse Hyperbolic Tangent.svg|thumb|upright=0.85|Rapidity is the value of {{math|artanh(''v'' / ''c'')}} for velocity {{mvar|v}} and speed of light {{mvar|c}}]]

In [[special relativity]], the classical concept of [[velocity]] is converted to '''rapidity''' to accommodate the limit determined by the [[speed of light]]. Velocities must be combined by Einstein's [[Velocity-addition formula#Special relativity|velocity-addition formula]]. For low speeds, rapidity and velocity are almost exactly proportional but, for higher velocities, rapidity takes a larger value, with the rapidity of light being infinite.

Mathematically, rapidity can be defined as the [[hyperbolic angle]] that differentiates two [[frames of reference]] in relative motion, each frame being associated with [[distance]] and [[time]] coordinates.

Using the [[inverse hyperbolic function]] {{math|artanh}}, the rapidity {{mvar|w}} corresponding to velocity {{mvar|v}} is:
<math display="block>w = \operatorname{artanh}(\frac{v}{c})</math>
where {{mvar|c}} is the speed of light.  Instead of {{mvar|w}}, some authors use {{mvar|ζ}}, {{mvar|η}}, {{mvar|ξ}}, {{mvar|ϕ}}, {{mvar|φ}}, or {{mvar|ψ}}.

For low speeds, by the [[small-angle approximation]], {{mvar|w}} is approximately {{math|''v'' / ''c''}}. Since in relativity any velocity {{mvar|v}} is constrained to the interval {{math|−''c'' < ''v'' < ''c''}} the ratio {{math|''v'' / ''c''}} satisfies {{math|−1 < ''v'' / ''c'' < 1}}. The inverse hyperbolic tangent has the unit interval {{math|(−1, 1)}} for its [[domain of a function|domain]] and the whole [[real line]] for its [[image (mathematics)|image]]; that is, the interval {{math|−''c'' < ''v'' < ''c''}} maps onto {{math|−∞ < ''w'' < ∞}}.

==History==
[[File:Add_velocity_Earth_POV.svg|thumb|Time ({{mvar|t}}) and space ({{mvar|x}}) axes: moving observers have primed or double primed axes]]
In 1908 [[Hermann Minkowski]] explained how the [[Lorentz transformation]] could be seen as simply a [[hyperbolic rotation]] of the [[Coordinate time|spacetime coordinates]], i.e., a rotation through an imaginary angle.<ref>[[Hermann Minkowski]] (1908) [https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Translation:The_Fundamental_Equations_for_Electromagnetic_Processes_in_Moving_Bodies Fundamental Equations for Electromagnetic Processes in Moving Bodies] via Wikisource</ref> This angle therefore represents (in one spatial dimension) a simple additive measure of the velocity between frames.<ref>Sommerfeld, Phys. Z 1909</ref> The rapidity parameter replacing velocity was introduced in 1910 by [[Vladimir Varićak]]<ref>[[Vladimir Varicak]] (1910) [https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Translation:Application_of_Lobachevskian_Geometry_in_the_Theory_of_Relativity Application of Lobachevskian Geometry in the Theory of Relativity] ''Physikalische Zeitschrift'' via [[Wikisource]]</ref> and by [[E. T. Whittaker]].<ref>[[E. T. Whittaker]] (1910) [[A History of the Theories of Aether and Electricity]], page 441.</ref> The parameter was named ''rapidity'' by [[Alfred Robb]] (1911)<ref>[[Alfred Robb]] (1911) ''Optical Geometry of Motion'' p.9</ref> and this term was adopted by many subsequent authors, such as [[Ludwik Silberstein]] (1914), [[Frank Morley]] (1936) and [[Wolfgang Rindler]] (2001).

===Minkowski diagram===

Rapidity is the parameter expressing variability of an event on the [[hyperbola]] which represents the future events one time unit away from the origin O. These events can be expressed {{math|(sinh ''w'', cosh ''w'')}} where {{math|sinh}} is the [[hyperbolic sine]] and {{math|cosh}} is the [[hyperbolic cosine]]. Note that as speed and {{mvar|w}} increase, the axes tilt toward the diagonal. In fact, they remain in a relation of [[hyperbolic orthogonality]] whatever the value of {{mvar|w}}. The appropriate {{mvar|x}}-axis is the ''hyperplane of simultaneity'' corresponding to rapidity {{mvar|w}} at the origin.

The hyperbola can be associated with the [[unit hyperbola]]. A moving [[reference frame]] sees the spacetime in the same way the rest frame does, so a transformation theory is necessary to explain the adaptation of one to the other. When the unit hyperbola is interpreted as a [[one-parameter group]] that [[group action|acts]] on the future, and correspondingly on the past and elsewhere, then the Minkowski configuration expresses the [[relativity of simultaneity]] and other features of relativity.

==Lorentz boost==
The transformations relating reference frames are associated with [[Hendrik Lorentz]]. To make a moving frame with rapidity {{mvar|w}} into the rest frame with [[perpendicular]] axes of time and space, one applies a [[hyperbolic rotation]] of parameter {{math|−''w''}}. Since&nbsp;{{math|1=cosh(−''w'') = cosh ''w''}} and&nbsp;{{math|1=sinh(−''w'') = −sinh ''w''}}, the following matrix representation of the hyperbolic rotation will bring the moving frame into perpendicularity (though all frames keep hyperbolic orthogonality since that relation is invariant under hyperbolic rotation).

A [[Lorentz boost]] is a vector-matrix product
<math display="block">
  \begin{pmatrix}
    c t' \\
    x'
  \end{pmatrix}
  =
  \begin{pmatrix}
    \cosh w & -\sinh w \\
    -\sinh w & \cosh w
  \end{pmatrix}
  \begin{pmatrix}
    ct \\
    x
  \end{pmatrix}
  = \mathbf \Lambda (w) 
  \begin{pmatrix}
    ct \\
    x
  \end{pmatrix}.</math>

The matrix {{math|'''Λ'''(''w'')}} is of the type <math>\begin{pmatrix} p & q \\ q & p \end{pmatrix} </math> with {{mvar|p}} and {{mvar|q}} satisfying {{math|1=''p''<sup>2</sup> – ''q''<sup>2</sup> = 1}}, so that {{math|(''p'', ''q'')}} lies on the [[unit hyperbola]]. Such matrices form the [[indefinite orthogonal group|indefinite orthogonal group O(1,1)]] with one-dimensional Lie algebra spanned by the anti-diagonal unit matrix, showing that the rapidity is the coordinate on this Lie algebra. In [[matrix exponential]] notation, {{math|'''Λ'''(''w'')}} can be expressed as <math>\mathbf \Lambda (w) = e^{\mathbf Z w}</math>, where {{math|'''Z'''}} is the negative of the anti-diagonal unit matrix
<math> \mathbf Z =
   \begin{pmatrix}
    0 & -1 \\
    -1 & 0
  \end{pmatrix} . </math> Since {{math|''Z''<sup>2</sup>}} is the identity, {{mvar|Z}} is a [[hyperbolic unit]].

===Velocity addition===

A key property of the matrix exponential is <math>e^{\mathbf X(s+t)}=e^{\mathbf Xs}e^{\mathbf Xt}</math> from which immediately follows that
<math display="block">\mathbf{\Lambda}(w_1 + w_2) = \mathbf{\Lambda}(w_1)\mathbf{\Lambda}(w_2).</math>
This establishes the useful additive property of rapidity: if {{math|A}}, {{math|B}} and {{math|C}} are [[frames of reference]], then
<math display="block"> w_{\text{AC}}= w_{\text{AB}} + w_{\text{BC}},</math>
where {{math|''w''<sub>PQ</sub>}} denotes the rapidity of a frame of reference {{math|Q}} relative to a frame of reference {{math|P}}. The simplicity of this formula contrasts with the complexity of the corresponding [[velocity-addition formula#Special theory of relativity|velocity-addition formula]].

As we can see from the Lorentz transformation above, the [[Lorentz factor]] identifies with {{math|cosh ''w''}}
<math display="block">\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2 / c^2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \beta^2}} \equiv \cosh w,</math>
so the rapidity {{mvar|w}} is implicitly used as a hyperbolic angle in the Lorentz transformation expressions using {{mvar|γ}} and {{mvar|β}}. We relate rapidities to the [[velocity-addition formula#Special theory of relativity|velocity-addition formula]]
<math display="block">u = \frac{u_1 + u_2}{1 + \frac{u_1 u_2}{c^2}}</math>
by recognizing
<math display="block">\beta_i = \frac{u_i}{c} = \tanh{w_i} </math>
and so
<math display="block">\tanh w = \frac{\tanh w_1 + \tanh w_2}{1 + \tanh w_1\tanh w_2}
= \tanh(w_1+ w_2)</math>

[[Proper acceleration]] (the acceleration 'felt' by the object being accelerated) is the rate of change of rapidity with respect to [[proper time]] (time as measured by the object undergoing acceleration itself). Therefore, the rapidity of an object in a given frame can be viewed simply as the velocity of that object as would be calculated non-relativistically by an inertial guidance system on board the object itself if it accelerated from rest in that frame to its given speed.

===Hyperbolic functions===

The product of {{mvar|β}} and {{mvar|γ}} appears frequently in the equations of special relativity.  As a result, some authors define an explicit parameter <math>\alpha</math> for this expression, which is, from above:
<math display="block"> \alpha = \beta \gamma = \tanh w \cosh w = \sinh w </math>

This relationship uses [[hyperbolic function]]s of the rapidity <math>w</math> to relate these parameters of special relativity, as Minkowski had observed:

<math display="block"> \alpha = \sinh w </math>
<math display="block"> \beta  = \tanh w </math>
<math display="block"> \gamma = \cosh w </math>

===Exponential and logarithmic relations===

From the above expressions we have
<math display="block">e^{w} = \cosh(w) + \sinh(w) = \gamma(1 + \beta) = \frac{ 1 + \beta }{ \sqrt{ 1 - \beta^2}  } = \sqrt \frac{1 + \tfrac{v}{c}}{1 - \tfrac{v}{c}},</math>
and thus
<math display="block">e^{-w} = \cosh(w) - \sinh(w) = \gamma(1 - \beta) = \frac{ 1 - \beta }{ \sqrt{ 1 - \beta^2}  }   = \sqrt \frac{1 - \tfrac{v}{c}}{1 + \tfrac{v}{c}}.</math>
or explicitly
<math display="block">w = \ln \left[\gamma(1 + \beta)\right] = -\ln \left[\gamma(1 - \beta)\right]  \, . </math>

===Doppler effect===
The [[relativistic Doppler effect|Doppler-shift]] factor, for the longitudinal case with source and receiver moving directly towards or away from each other, that is associated with rapidity {{mvar|w}} is <math>k = e^w</math>.

==In experimental particle physics==
The energy {{mvar|E}} and scalar momentum {{math|{{!}}'''p'''{{!}}}} of a particle of non-zero (rest) mass {{mvar|m}} are given by:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
E &= \gamma mc^2 \\
\left| \mathbf p \right| &= \gamma mv.
\end{align}</math>
With the definition of {{mvar|w}}
<math display="block"> w = \operatorname{artanh} \frac{v}{c}  = \operatorname{artanh} \beta,</math>
and thus with
<math display="block">\cosh w = \cosh \left( \operatorname{artanh} \frac{v}{c} \right) = \frac {1}{ \sqrt { 1- \frac{v^2}{c^2} }} = \gamma</math>
<math display="block">\sinh w =  \sinh \left( \operatorname{artanh} \frac{v}{c} \right) = \frac {\frac{v}{c}}{ \sqrt { 1- \frac{v^2}{c^2} }} = \beta \gamma = \alpha ,</math>
the energy and scalar momentum can be written as:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
E &= m c^2 \cosh w \\
\left| \mathbf p \right| &= m c \, \sinh w.
\end{align} </math>

So, rapidity can be calculated from measured energy and momentum by
<math display="block"> w = \operatorname{artanh} \frac{| \mathbf p | c}{E}= \frac{1}{2} \ln \frac{E + | \mathbf p | c}{E - | \mathbf p | c} = \ln \frac{E + | \mathbf p | c}{ mc^2}  ~.</math>

However, experimental particle physicists often use a modified definition of rapidity relative to a beam axis
<math display="block">y = \frac{1}{2} \ln \frac{E + p_z c}{E - p_z c} ,</math>
where {{math|''p''<sub>''z''</sub>}} is the component of momentum along the beam axis.<ref>Amsler, C. ''et al.'', [http://pdg.lbl.gov/2009/reviews/rpp2009-rev-kinematics.pdf "The Review of Particle Physics"], ''Physics Letters B'' '''667''' (2008) 1, Section 38.5.2</ref>  This is the rapidity of the boost along the beam axis which takes an observer from the lab frame to a frame in which the particle moves only perpendicular to the beam.  Related to this is the concept of [[pseudorapidity]].

Rapidity relative to a beam axis can also be expressed as
<math display="block">y = \ln \frac{E + p_z c}{\sqrt{m^2c^4+p_T^2 c^2} } ~.</math>
